title: Mestrezat and Perkins: refuge/access justifies — special persuasion is perfection
source_text: LII. Atque haec quoque fuit proculdubio sententia viri celeberrimi Joannis Mestrezatii, qui ut supra observavimus, fidem justificantem definit variis in locis, Perfugium peccatoris poenitentis ad Dei misericordiam in Christo. Nec etiam alia mens fuit Guil. Perkinsii, ut videre est ex iis quae docet de ortu & gradibus fidei justificantis. Postquam enim quatuor gradus, sive motus cordis in fide observavit, quorum primus est notitia Evangelii, & assensus illi praebitus per Spiritus Sancti illuminationem. Secundus spes veniae, qua peccator, etsi nondum sentit remissum esse peccatum, remissibile tamen esse credit. Tertius, esuries & vehemens expetitio gratiae, quae est oblata in Christo Jesu. Quartus, accessus ad thronum gratiae, ut apprehenso ibidem Christo, inveniamus misericordiam apud Deum, subjungit hunc gradum sequi immediate remissionem peccatorum coram Deo, quae est ipsa nostra justificatio. Et tandem succedere quintum & summum fidei gradum, qui est specialis persuasio cordi a Spiritu Sancto impressa, qua promissiones Evangelicas quisque sibi speciatim applicat. Nam accessus ille ad thronum gratiae, ut apprehenso ibidem Christo, inveniamus misericordiam apud Deum, est illa ipsa fiducia perfugii, quae a nobis modo descripta est, quam immediate, juxta authorem illum, sequitur justificatio. Specialis autem persuasio, qua promissiones Evangelicas quisque sibi speciatim applicat, non aliud est quam quae dicitur fiducia sensus, quae ex mente Perkinsii, justificationem jam factam consequitur, ac proinde non est illius organum, nec ad intimam fidei essentiam, sine qua fides, nequidem ad momentum constare potest; sed solum ad fidei perfectionem pertinet; ut supra quoque vidimus Perkinsium docentem.
pass_a_gloss: And this also was without doubt the opinion of the most celebrated man John Mestrezat, who as we observed above defines justifying faith in various places as the Refuge of the penitent sinner to God's mercy in Christ. Nor was William Perkins's mind otherwise, as may be seen from what he teaches concerning the rise and degrees of justifying faith. For after he observed four degrees, or motions of the heart in faith — of which the first is knowledge of the Gospel, and the assent given to it by the illumination of the Holy Spirit; the second hope of pardon, by which the sinner, although he does not yet feel that sin has been remitted, yet believes it to be remissible; the third, hunger and vehement desire for the grace offered in Christ Jesus; the fourth, access to the throne of grace, that having apprehended Christ there we may find mercy with God — he subjoins that this degree is immediately followed by remission of sins before God, which is our very justification. And at length there succeeds a fifth and highest degree of faith, which is a special persuasion impressed on the heart by the Holy Spirit, by which each applies the Evangelical promises to himself specially. For that access to the throne of grace, that having apprehended Christ there we may find mercy with God, is that very trust of refuge which we have just described, which according to that author justification immediately follows. But the special persuasion by which each applies the Evangelical promises to himself specially is nothing other than what is called trust of sense, which on Perkins's mind follows justification already made, and therefore is not its organ, nor pertains to the inmost essence of faith without which faith cannot stand even for a moment; but only to the perfection of faith — as we also saw Perkins teaching above.
pass_b_english: Mestrezat: justifying faith = penitent’s refuge to God’s mercy in Christ.
Perkins’s fourth degree (access to the throne, apprehend Christ) = fiducia of refuge — justification follows at once.
Fifth/special Spirit-persuasion applying promises = fiducia of sense — follows justification; perfection, not essence.
